clinicalScope: Acute tissue inflammation in adult patients presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Acute Inflammation
subject: Pathology
summary: Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection, producing redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. In low‑resource settings the common triggers are infections, trauma and tropical diseases, and clinicians must diagnose and manage it with limited investigations.

sections.p: Inflammation is a complex biological response of vascular tissues to harmful stimuli, aimed at eliminating the cause and initiating repair. It is classified as acute (minutes to weeks) or chronic (weeks to years).
b: Cardinal signs: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa
Acute inflammation: rapid onset, neutrophil predominance, exudate formation
Chronic inflammation: slower, mononuclear cells, fibrosis
Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is a severe form with organ dysfunction

sections.p: In the East African context the most frequent precipitants are infectious (bacterial, viral, parasitic), traumatic, and toxin‑related.
b: Bacterial skin/soft‑tissue infection (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes)
Malaria‑related hepatic or splenic inflammation
Trauma from road‑traffic accidents or agricultural injuries
Traditional herbal remedies causing chemical irritation
HIV‑associated opportunistic infections
Tuberculosis causing granulomatous inflammation

sections.p: The inflammatory cascade proceeds through vascular, cellular and molecular phases that together produce the clinical signs.
b: 1. Tissue injury → release of DAMPs (damage‑associated molecular patterns)
2. Vasodilation mediated by histamine, prostaglandins → rubor and calor
3. Increased vascular permeability → tumor (edema) and exudate
4. Leukocyte margination, rolling, adhesion (selectins, integrins)
5. Neutrophil migration (chemotaxis) and phagocytosis of microbes
6. Release of cytokines (IL‑1, TNF‑α) amplifies response and can cause fever
7. Resolution: apoptosis of neutrophils, macrophage‑mediated clearance, tissue repair

sections.p: Visible changes depend on organ and severity; acute inflammation typically appears red, swollen, and warm.
b: Skin: erythema, edema, possible purulent discharge
Viscera: hyperemic, edematous serosa, possible fibrinous exudate
Joint: effusion with straw‑coloured fluid
Lung: consolidation with increased firmness

sections.p: Histology reveals characteristic cellular infiltrates and vascular changes.
b: Dilated capillaries with endothelial swelling
Leukocyte infiltrate: neutrophils early, then macrophages
Fibrin deposition in severe cases (exudate)
Edema in interstitial spaces
In chronic phase: lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibroblast proliferation

sections.p: Patients present with local and systemic signs that guide bedside assessment.
b: Localized pain, tenderness, warmth, swelling, erythema
Reduced range of motion if peri‑articular
Fever, tachycardia, malaise indicating systemic involvement
Signs of SIRS: HR > 90, RR > 20, Temp > 38 °C or < 36 °C, WBC > 12 000 or < 4 000
Intra‑abdominal inflammation: guarding, rebound tenderness

sections.p: Laboratory and bedside tests confirm the presence, severity and likely cause of inflammation.

t.b: Is there leukocytosis or left shift? ↑ neutrophils supports bacterial infection; lymphocytosis suggests viral or TB
What organism is causing infection? Guides antibiotic choice
Is there an abscess or fluid collection? Detects hypoechoic collection with posterior enhancement
Do systemic signs meet SIRS criteria? Determines need for urgent escalation

sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of local signs and systemic response.
b: Mild: localized signs, no fever, normal vitals
Moderate: pronounced swelling, pain, fever ≥ 38 °C, HR > 100
Severe (SIRS/early sepsis): fever or hypothermia, HR > 120, RR > 30, hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg)
Chronic stage: fibrosis, loss of function after weeks

sections.p: If untreated, acute inflammation can progress to tissue destruction and systemic illness.
b: Abscess formation requiring drainage
Necrotizing fasciitis – rapid spread, high mortality
Sepsis and multi‑organ failure
Fibrosis leading to chronic pain or functional loss
Infection spread (e.g., cellulitis → osteomyelitis)

sections.p: Management targets the inciting cause, modulates the inflammatory response, and prevents complications.
b: 1. Source control: drainage of pus, debridement of necrotic tissue
2. Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) pending culture; adjust to local resistance patterns
3. Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs in renal insufficiency or active GI ulcer
4. Fluid resuscitation for severe SIRS (30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus if hypotensive)
5. Monitor vitals, urine output, and CRP daily
6. Consider corticosteroids only for specific immune‑mediated inflammation (e.g., severe cellulitis with extensive edema) and when infection is ruled out

sections.p: Linking bedside findings with pathology helps anticipate disease course.
b: Purulent discharge → neutrophil‑rich exudate, bacterial infection
Warm, red skin with systemic fever → acute bacterial cellulitis
Non‑purulent, indurated swelling with low-grade fever → tuberculous or fungal inflammation
Rapid progression, severe pain, crepitus → necrotizing fasciitis (gas‑forming organisms)

sections.p: A systematic bedside assessment ensures no key feature is missed.
b: History: onset, trauma, wound exposure, fever pattern, HIV/TB status, recent travel, herbal medicine use
Inspection: colour, swelling, discharge, skin breaks
Palpation: tenderness, warmth, fluctuance, induration
Percussion (abdomen): guarding, rebound
Vital signs: temperature, HR, RR, BP, mental status
Decision tree: if SIRS present → start IV fluids, broad antibiotics, consider ICU

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading redness or pain, fever > 39 °C, hypotension, altered mental status, or signs of necrotizing infection

faq.a: Cytokines like IL‑1 and TNF‑α act on the hypothalamus to raise the set‑point, producing fever.

faq.q: Can NSAIDs be used in all acute inflammations?
faq.a: No; avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment, active GI ulcer, or when they may mask worsening infection.

faq.q: What is the first step if an abscess is suspected but imaging is unavailable?
faq.a: Perform bedside needle aspiration; if pus is obtained, drain and start antibiotics.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with a rapidly expanding painful leg swelling, fever = 38.8 °C, HR = 115. What is the next immediate management step? — Initiate IV fluids and broad‑spectrum antibiotics, arrange urgent surgical drainage.

Explain how you would differentiate cellulitis from early necrotizing fasciitis at the bedside. — Look for severe pain out of proportion, tense edema, bullae, crepitus, systemic toxicity; necrotizing fasciitis often shows rapid progression and gas on palpation.

A patient with HIV presents with chronic non‑purulent joint swelling. Which inflammatory pattern is most likely and why? — Chronic mononuclear infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages) suggests tuberculous or fungal arthritis, common in immunocompromised hosts.

Why is source control more important than antibiotics in severe soft‑tissue infection? — Removing the nidus (abscess, necrotic tissue) eliminates the stimulus for ongoing inflammation; antibiotics alone cannot penetrate devitalized tissue.

What are the cardinal signs of acute inflammation and which of them are mediated by vascular changes? — Rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa; rubor, calor, and tumor result from vasodilation and increased permeability.

A child with malaria develops splenomegaly and left upper quadrant pain. How does inflammation contribute to this presentation? — Parasitic sequestration triggers cytokine release, causing splenic congestion, edema, and pain.
List three local factors that impede resolution of inflammation in low‑resource settings. — Delayed presentation, limited access to imaging/drainage, inadequate antibiotic supply.

When is corticosteroid therapy indicated in acute inflammation? — When inflammation is immune‑mediated (e.g., severe allergic cellulitis) and infection has been excluded; not in uncontrolled bacterial infection.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: When a patient presents with a painful, swollen area, the clinician must separate simple cellulitis from more aggressive processes and identify systemic involvement.
b: Onset: rapid (hours) suggests necrotizing infection; slower (days) favours cellulitis.
Pain: out‑of‑proportion to visible signs points to deep tissue necrosis.
Systemic features: fever, tachycardia, hypotension indicate SIRS or sepsis.
Risk factors: diabetes, HIV, trauma, recent herbal application, immunosuppression.
Progression: spreading erythema >2 cm/h, skin bullae, crepitus, anesthesia over the area.
Local warmth: compare with contralateral site; marked increase supports active inflammation.
Palpation: firm, tender induration suggests fascia involvement; fluctuation indicates abscess.
Bedside tests limitations: the “finger‑test” (pain on palpation) cannot differentiate bacterial species or depth of infection.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, choose tests that answer the key clinical question while recognising what to do when a test is unavailable.

t.b: Is there a systemic inflammatory response? Neutrophil count >7 ×10⁹/L and left shift support bacterial infection; leukopenia may suggest overwhelming sepsis.
Is tissue hypoperfusion present? Lactate ≥2 mmol/L indicates early shock; ≥4 mmol/L signals severe sepsis requiring urgent resuscitation.
What is the causative organism? Positive growth guides targeted antibiotics; if unavailable, start broad‑spectrum empiric therapy based on local flora.

t.a: Wound swab or aspirate Gram stain
t.b: Is there a predominance of Gram‑positive cocci (Staph/Strep) or Gram‑negative rods? Guides empiric choice; a paucity of organisms may indicate necrotizing fasciitis.
Is there a fluid collection or fascial thickening? Hypoechoic fluid with “dirty shadowing” suggests abscess; loss of fascial plane indicates necrotizing infection.
Is there subcutaneous gas? Presence of radiolucent streaks strongly supports necrotizing fasciitis.
Rely on clinical scoring (e.g., LRINEC – use available labs) and early surgical consultation; do not delay source control awaiting results.

sections.p: Classification combines clinical pattern, depth of tissue involvement and systemic impact.
b: Cellulitis – superficial dermal and subcutaneous infection, no fascial involvement, usually <5 cm spread per hour.
Necrotizing fasciitis – rapid fascial necrosis, pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity; LRINEC score ≥6 suggests high risk.
Abscess – localized pus collection, fluctuant on palpation, may coexist with cellulitis.
Severe systemic inflammation – SIRS criteria (≥2: temperature >38 °C or <36 °C, HR >90, RR >20 or PaCO₂ <32 mmHg, WBC >12 ×10⁹/L or <4 ×10⁹/L).
Stage I (mild) – limited erythema, no systemic signs; treat with oral antibiotics.
Stage II (moderate) – extensive erythema, fever, elevated CRP; require IV antibiotics and possible incision‑drainage.
Stage III (severe) – necrosis, gas, organ dysfunction; urgent surgical debridement plus ICU support.

sections.p: Several other pathologies can mimic acute soft‑tissue inflammation, especially in tropical, low‑resource settings.

t.b: Points to it: unilateral leg swelling, pain on calf compression, risk factors (immobility, pregnancy). Separate by Homan’s sign, duplex ultrasound; DVT lacks erythema and warmth.
Points to it: sudden mono‑articular pain, tophi, hyperuricemia. Joint aspiration shows negatively birefringent needle‑shaped crystals; inflammation is sterile.
Points to it: linear red streaks following lymphatics, often after skin breach. No fascial thickening; ultrasound shows superficial vein inflammation, not deep fascial loss.
Points to it: muscle tenderness, elevated CK, systemic viral prodrome. MRI shows muscle edema without fascial gas; cultures are negative.
Points to it: sharply demarcated, raised erythema on face or legs, often Streptococcus pyogenes. No deep fascial involvement; responds rapidly to penicillin.

sections.p: Begin with rapid assessment, then definitive care, monitor, and know when to refer. This ladder keeps patients safe while using limited resources.
b: 1. Immediate ABCs: airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen if SpO₂<94%. 2. Obtain vital signs, pain score, and local exam; note redness, warmth, swelling, and any crepitus. 3. Start empiric broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics covering common skin flora (e.g., ceftriaxone + clindamycin) unless contraindicated. 4. Initiate fluid resuscitation with crystalloids to maintain MAP >65 m

t.b: Ceftriaxone covers gram‑negative rods; clindamycin blocks toxin production and covers anaerobes.
Avoid monotherapy with narrow agents (e.g., penicillin alone) in severe infections.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Know the common side effects and interactions of the main drugs used in inflammation management.
b: 1. Ceftriaxone: biliary sludge, rash; monitor liver enzymes and watch for jaundice. 2. Clindamycin: C. difficile colitis; advise patient to report diarrhoea and consider stool test. 3. NSAIDs: GI ulcer, renal impairment; use proton‑pump inhibitor if risk factors present. 4. Systemic steroids: hyperglycaemia, infection flare; check blood glucose and counsel on infection signs. 5

t.b: Use PPIs if history of ulcers or concurrent steroids.
Check fasting glucose; adjust diabetic meds.

sections.p: Recognise early warning signs that require urgent escalation to prevent morbidity and mortality.
b: 1. Rapid spread of erythema beyond initial area. 2. New bullae or necrotic skin. 3. Systemic signs: tachycardia >120 bpm, hypotension, altered mental status. 4. Rising creatinine or oliguria indicating renal failure. 5. Persistent fever >48 h despite antibiotics. 6. Worsening pain out of proportion to exam. 7. Positive air‑crepitus on palpation. 8. If any of these occur, transf

t.b: Any sign of systemic toxicity or necrosis warrants transfer.

sections.p: Patient comorbidities and local practices can alter presentation and treatment response.
b: 1. HIV: higher risk of opportunistic infections; use broader coverage and monitor CD4. 2. TB: granulomatous inflammation may mimic chronic abscess; consider sputum PCR. 3. Malnutrition: impaired wound healing; provide protein supplementation. 4. Pregnancy: avoid nephrotoxic drugs; use penicillin‑based regimens. 5. Diabetes: ↑ infection severity; control glucose tightly. 6. Herb

t.b: Reduce ceftriaxone dose in CKD; avoid NSAIDs in liver disease.
Artemisinin can potentiate cytochrome P450; monitor drug levels.

sections.p: Tailor management for vulnerable populations in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Children: use weight‑based dosing; avoid NSAIDs if dehydrated. 2. Elderly: polypharmacy risk; review all meds for interactions. 3. HIV patients: consider drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals. 4. Low‑resource settings: prioritize empiric therapy, use available antibiotics, and ensure basic wound care. 5. Pregnant women: use penicillin or cephalosporins; avoid fluoroqui

t.b: Penicillin or cephalosporin preferred in pregnancy; avoid fluoroquinolones.
Use simple bedside tests (e.g., pulse oximetry, temperature) when labs unavailable.

facts: Acute inflammation onset: minutes to hours; chronic: days to weeks.
Neutrophil predominance in exudate indicates acute phase; lymphocytes/macrophages indicate chronic.
Temperature >38 °C with tachycardia >90 bpm and respiratory rate >20/min meets SIRS criteria.
WBC count >12 ×10⁹/L with left shift supports bacterial acute inflammation.
Granuloma formation requires ≥2 weeks of persistent antigenic stimulus.
Fibrinous exudate appears as a thin, yellowish layer on serosal surfaces.
Resolution requires macrophage clearance and release of lipoxins, resolvins, protectins.
In low‑resource hospitals, delayed source control >24 h raises mortality >30 % in necrotizing fasciitis.
Corticosteroids are indicated in acute severe inflammation when benefits outweigh infection risk, e.g., meningitis adjunct.

mnemonics.t: Calor, Rubor, Tumor, Dolor – the four classic vascular signs of acute inflammation.
Vasodilation, Increased permeability, Neutrophil recruitment – key steps in the vascular phase.

vivas.q: Define the five cardinal signs of inflammation and indicate which are primarily vascular.
vivas.a: Rubor (redness) and calor (heat) are due to vasodilation; tumor (swelling) from increased permeability; dolor (pain) from nerve irritation; functio laesa (loss of function) is a consequence.

vivas.q: What laboratory thresholds support a diagnosis of SIRS?
vivas.a: Temperature >38 °C or <36 °C, heart rate >90 bpm, respiratory rate >20/min or PaCO₂ <32 mmHg, WBC >12 ×10⁹/L or <4 ×10⁹/L or >10 % bands.

vivas.q: Explain how to differentiate cellulitis from early necrotizing fasciitis at the bedside.
vivas.a: Cellulitis: diffuse erythema, tenderness, preserved skin integrity, no severe pain out of proportion. Necrotizing fasciitis: severe pain beyond erythema, rapid progression, tense edema, bullae, crepitus, systemic toxicity.

vivas.q: Why is source control more important than antibiotics in severe soft‑tissue infection?
vivas.a: Removing necrotic tissue eliminates the bacterial nidus and improves antibiotic penetration; delays increase mortality regardless of drug choice.

vivas.q: When is corticosteroid therapy indicated in acute inflammation?
vivas.a: When the inflammatory response threatens organ function (e.g., bacterial meningitis, severe asthma, autoimmune flare) and benefits outweigh infection risk; not in uncontrolled sepsis without source control.

vivas.q: An immunocompromised patient develops progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy without inflammation. Which virus is reactivated?
A physician says, 'You are not in pain, it is just inflammation.' Which communication principle is breached?
vivas.a: Empathy – dismissing the patient’s subjective experience undermines therapeutic relationship.

vivas.q: Rapid onset and severity of radiation‑induced mucositis are due to what cellular process?
vivas.a: Direct DNA damage to basal epithelial cells leading to apoptosis and loss of mucosal barrier.

vivas.q: Chronic gingival inflammation with plasma cells and lymphocytes reflects which type of immune response?
vivas.a: Chronic cell‑mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity with a dominant Th1/Th17 profile.

vivas.q: Mechanism behind migratory polyarthritis after streptococcal pharyngitis with high ASO titers?
vivas.a: Molecular mimicry leading to immune complex deposition (type III hypersensitivity) in joints.

vivas.q: Primary pathological site causing airway obstruction in croup (steeple sign)?
vivas.a: Subglottic mucosal edema and inflammation narrowing the airway lumen.

vivas.q: In ulcerative colitis, what histological feature defines the disease?
Metabolic pathway that generates uric acid crystals in gout?
vivas.a: Purine degradation via xanthine oxidase converting hypoxanthine to xanthine to uric acid.

vivas.q: List common causes of acute gastric inflammation.
vivas.a: Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, acute stress (e.g., burns), alcohol binge, severe infection.

vivas.q: Key steps of coagulation that aid immune defense after barrier breach.
vivas.a: Fibrin mesh traps microbes, and thrombin-generated fibrinogen fragments act as chemotactic signals for neutrophils.

vivas.q: What are three local factors that impede resolution of inflammation in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: Persistent bacterial load due to inadequate debridement, ongoing tissue hypoxia, and lack of access to anti‑inflammatory agents.

mcqs.q: A 42‑year‑old farmer presents with a painful, rapidly expanding leg swelling, fever 38.9 °C, HR 110 bpm. Which finding most strongly suggests necrotizing fasciitis?
o: Pain out of proportion to visual signs
Erythema limited to the area of swelling
mcqs.e: Severe pain disproportionate to exam is classic for necrotizing fasciitis.

mcqs.q: Which cytokine is primarily responsible for fever in acute inflammation?
mcqs.e: IL‑1 acts on the hypothalamus to raise the set‑point.

mcqs.q: In a patient with HIV and chronic non‑purulent knee swelling, the predominant inflammatory pattern is:
mcqs.e: Chronic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates are typical of indolent joint inflammation in immunocompromise.

mcqs.q: Which of the following best describes the exudate in serous inflammation?
mcqs.e: Serous exudate is thin, clear, and low in protein.

mcqs.q: A child with malaria develops splenomegaly and left upper quadrant pain. The splenic inflammation is mainly due to:
o: Direct parasite invasion of splenic parenchyma
Hyperplasia of macrophages clearing parasitized RBCs
mcqs.e: Malaria triggers massive macrophage activity to remove infected red cells, causing congestion and inflammation.

mcqs.q: Which drug class is first‑line for preventing further joint damage in chronic rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic inflammatory disease?
mcqs.e: Disease‑modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are the cornerstone of long‑term control.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old male farmer presents with a 2‑day history of a painful, swollen right lower leg. The skin is erythematous, warm, and there are tense bullae. He is febrile (38.7 °C) and tachycardic (115 bpm). No obvious wound is seen.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What immediate management step should be taken?
qs.a: Urgent surgical exploration and debridement plus broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics.

qs.q: Which bedside sign helps differentiate it from cellulitis?
qs.a: Pain out of proportion to the visible erythema and presence of tense bullae or crepitus.

cases.v: A 45‑year‑old woman with known HIV (CD4 150 cells/µL) reports a 3‑month history of painless swelling of the left knee. Examination shows a mildly effused joint without warmth or erythema. Synovial fluid analysis reveals a lymphocyte‑predominant, sterile exudate.

qs.q: What is the most likely inflammatory pattern?
Which investigation would best confirm the underlying cause?
qs.a: PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in synovial fluid.

qs.q: What is the first‑line treatment if TB arthritis is confirmed?
qs.a: Standard anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 6‑9 months plus joint physiotherapy.

mistakes: Confusing cellulitis with necrotizing fasciitis and delaying surgical referral.
Relying solely on temperature to diagnose SIRS without considering heart rate, respiratory rate, and WBC.
Prescribing antibiotics without first achieving source control in deep soft‑tissue infections.
Using corticosteroids in uncontrolled sepsis without ruling out active infection.
Omitting fibrinous exudate description when describing serosal inflammation.
Failing to mention the role of DAMPs in initiating sterile inflammation.
Misidentifying chronic granulomatous inflammation as acute neutrophilic response.
Neglecting to assess for HIV or TB in chronic joint effusions in low‑resource settings.
